open-question.question: The lowest-numbered pick needs a rule for reading the number out of milestone_<NN>_<slug>, and the only such rule in the skill today (strip leading zeros, compare as integers) lives inside the multiple-candidate branch that is being removed. Does the integer rule survive as a standalone sentence of the candidate step, and does a directory whose prefix does not parse as an integer get skipped or stop the run?
open-question.recommendation: It moves the existing sentence out of the branch being removed, matches define's own parse rule so ordering holds past milestone 99, adds no third stop the goal forbids, and a misnamed directory sits visibly in the tree so an advisory would only repeat what git already holds.
open-question.alternative: Keep the zero-stripped integer rule as a standalone sentence of the candidate step, and define candidates as directories matching `milestone_<digits>_<slug>` only. A directory whose prefix is not all digits never matches the pattern, so it is quietly left out of the candidate set. It is the smallest edit that still orders correctly past milestone 99. It moves the existing sentence out of the branch being removed, matches the parse rule `/define-milestone-goal` already uses for max-plus-one, and adds no new stop to a skill whose goal allows exactly two. A misnamed directory (for example `milestone_3a_fix` or one created by hand) is ignored with no signal. The user may then wonder why a milestone they defined is never activated, and the skill leaves no trace explaining it.

Keep the integer rule as a standalone sentence, and make any `milestone_*` directory whose number does not parse as an integer stop the run with a message naming the directory, before anything is written. A malformed directory is never silently passed over or mis-ordered. The user hears about it right away, and an unattended `claude -p` chain fails loudly instead of activating some other milestone. It adds a third stop condition when the goal says the skill stops in only two cases, so the goal text or a recorded decision would need to widen that. It also halts every activation over a stray directory that `/define-milestone-goal`'s naming rule should never have produced.

Keep the integer rule as a standalone sentence, leave directories whose prefix does not parse out of the candidate set, and have the run print one advisory line naming each skipped directory next to the terse `Milestone activated.` line. The run still finishes under the goal's two stop cases, and the user still learns that a directory was ignored. This fits the terse-reporting rule's allowance for decision-critical advisories that git does not record. It adds a second line to the success-path output and a new reporting branch to the skill, all for a case the project's own naming makes nearly impossible. It also stretches the "one fixed identifier-free status line" rule toward per-item output.

Drop the explicit number rule and pick the candidate whose directory name sorts first. This relies on `/define-milestone-goal` always zero-padding the number to two digits. The candidate step needs no parse sentence and no handling for unparseable prefixes, so it is the shortest possible text. Ordering breaks at milestone 100: `milestone_100_…` sorts before `milestone_99_…` because define pads to two digits, not three. The order would also differ silently from the integer rule `/define-milestone-goal` uses, and a misnamed directory would land at an arbitrary place in the order.

open-question.question: Once the skill only proceeds when the pointer reads none and always overwrites it with a path, the commit procedure's dirty-own-path guard can no longer fire, so the "No change — the pointer already named that milestone" line in the confirm step becomes unreachable. Does that branch stay as a defensive fallback or is it removed along with the prompts?
open-question.recommendation: The guard can still fire on an uncommitted reset of the pointer, so the branch stays to honour the one-distinct-no-op-line rule every committing skill follows, and its reason is rewritten to say only that the pointer line already matched the last commit, dropping the claim step 1 has just contradicted.
open-question.alternative: Keep the no-change branch in step 5 but rewrite its example reason to the one case that can still reach it. The pointer the skill wrote matches the last commit because an uncommitted edit had reset it to none. The skill still prints no terse line and commits nothing. The skill still says exactly what happens when the guard fires, so it never prints `Milestone activated.` for a run that recorded nothing. The message also tells the truth about the one real cause, and the reporting shape stays consistent with the other committing skills. It adds prose about a hand-edit case that almost never happens, to a skill whose milestone goal is simplification. It also puts a claim about how the workflow is misused into runtime prose, and that claim has to be kept accurate if the pointer or commit mechanics change later.

Leave step 5's no-change branch as it is, with its current example line `No change — the pointer already named that milestone; nothing committed.`, and remove only the confirmation and choice prompts from step 2. This is the smallest edit. The skill keeps the same reporting shape as every other committing skill (define-milestone-goal, modify-milestone-goal, specify-milestone-starting-state, init-milestone-base-workflow, and review-milestone-requirements all carry a distinct no-change line for when the dirty-own-path guard fires). It also still covers a case the premise overlooks. Say the committed README already points at milestone X and someone resets it to none by hand without committing. The skill then writes X back, the file matches HEAD again, `git status --porcelain` shows it clean, and the guard fires. So the branch is rare but can still be reached. The reason in the example line no longer fits how the guard can actually fire. Step 1 has just confirmed the pointer read none, so "the pointer already named that milestone" contradicts what the skill saw. A reader could also take the branch as a sign that re-activating the current milestone is still a supported path, when the non-interactive design rules that out.

Delete step 5's no-change paragraph along with the prompts. The skill then prints only `Milestone activated.`, and the rare case where nothing gets committed is left to the commit procedure's own instruction to report the no-op and return cleanly. The skill gets shorter and matches the new design, where every run that passes step 1 writes a new path and commits it. That removes the misleading reason and the idea that re-activation is still possible. The uncommitted-reset case can still reach the guard, and step 5 would then no longer say what to print. The runner could print `Milestone activated.` for a run that committed nothing, or produce a free-form message. That breaks the rule that no-op passes print one distinct line. It is also the only committing skill that would lack a no-change branch.

open-question.question: With the choice removed, a defined milestone that the user no longer wants but never finished is picked on every run and blocks every higher-numbered one, since the skill stops only on a non-none pointer or on no candidate. Is that accepted as-is, with deleting the directory as the way out, or does the skill or its documentation need to state how to skip such a milestone?

recommendation.option: Document removal as the way out

open-question.recommendation: CONTRIBUTING step 2 now advises leaving exactly the directory the new rule would activate first, so that sentence must require the revert and the skill-reference entry names directory removal as the way out, while the runtime file stays free of user-facing prose and no new argument or invented finish is added.

alternative.id: Document removal as the way out

open-question.alternative: Keep the lowest-numbered pick unchanged and say how to skip a milestone in the documentation only. The goto-next-milestone entry in docs/skill-reference.md would state that an unwanted milestone is skipped by removing its directory, for example by reverting its Milestone-definition commit. The CONTRIBUTING.md sentence that allows leaving an abandoned reservation as a candidate would be corrected to require the revert. It tells users about the trap where they look for skill behaviour, and it fixes the one existing sentence that now advises the wrong thing. The runtime SKILL.md gets no user-facing prose, which matches the project rule that runtime files carry only what the runner needs. It reaches outside the goal's file list, since CONTRIBUTING.md is not named there. Whether that edit belongs in this milestone depends on how the scope of out-of-list documents is settled. Also, deleting the highest-numbered directory lets /define-milestone-goal's max-plus-one rule reissue that number later.

Keep the behaviour the goal describes and add nothing. An unwanted milestone that was never finished stays the lowest-numbered pick until someone removes its directory, for example by reverting its Milestone-definition commit. Neither the skill nor any document mentions this way out. It needs no extra edits beyond the files the goal already lists. It keeps the milestone's scope to removing the two prompts, and the SKILL.md stays free of prose meant for the user rather than the runner. The trap is invisible, and the project already sets it. CONTRIBUTING.md step 2 says an abandoned contribution may be left on main "as a /goto-next-milestone candidate". Under the new rule, that directory would be activated by the next headless "Starting a milestone" chain in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, or by a contributor's first goto run, in place of the intended milestone, and nothing would warn anyone.

Treat an unwanted milestone as something to close rather than delete, and document that. The user lets /goto-next-milestone activate it, clears or moves any remaining tasks, and runs /finish-current-milestone. That adds a Milestone History entry and a Completed Milestones row, which removes it from the candidate set while keeping the directory and its history. It needs no change to any skill and keeps every defined milestone's directory and number in the tree. Nothing is deleted, and no number can be reissued. The history would record a milestone that accomplished nothing as done. That conflicts with finish's rule that summary bullets are never invented accomplishments, and it blurs Milestone History for later capture and release notes. It also takes three steps, including a commit that activates a milestone nobody wants.

Add a non-interactive override: /goto-next-milestone accepts an optional milestone directory or number. With it, the skill activates that milestone. Without it, the skill keeps the lowest-numbered pick, so a user can step past an abandoned milestone without removing it. It fixes the blocking directly while staying prompt-free. The override also works in headless chains and on a contributor's branch, where a stale reservation on main would otherwise be picked first. It adds a feature the goal never asked for and grows the milestone's scope. The skill currently takes no arguments, so this means argument validation and matching against done milestones, plus new text in both documents. It also does not stop the no-argument run, including the headless chain, from picking the abandoned milestone.

open-question.question: The README template in init-milestone-base-workflow says the ## Completed Milestones table is written by /goto-next-milestone, but the finish skill writes it and goto-next-milestone only reads it at most. Is correcting that note in scope for this milestone, given it sits outside the files the goal lists?

recommendation.option: Delete the note in this milestone

open-question.recommendation: The finish skill's own step already states that it writes both records, so the note is a cross-reference that can only go stale again, and deleting it removes the false claim now, in the rebuild the goal already requires, without wording that hangs on how done milestones are matched.

alternative.id: Delete the note in this milestone

open-question.alternative: In this milestone, remove the blockquote under the README template in `core/skills/init-milestone-base-workflow/SKILL.md` instead of rewording it. The template's two sections stay, and no sentence names which skill writes or reads them. It removes the stale claim, and nothing is left that can go stale again whenever a skill's relationship to the README changes. The sentence's wording also no longer depends on how `/goto-next-milestone` detects done milestones. The finish skill already creates the `## Completed Milestones` section when it is missing, so the "neither skill fails" warning protects less than it claims. It is still a change outside the files the goal lists, so it needs a decision that widens the scope. It also drops the only line telling a runner of the bootstrap why the README keeps two overlapping records of done milestones. A later editor could then merge or drop one of them without seeing that a skill depends on it.

alternative.id: Correct the note in this milestone

open-question.alternative: Rewrite the attribution in the bootstrap README template note in `core/skills/init-milestone-base-workflow/SKILL.md` so it says `/finish-current-milestone` writes both the `## Milestone History` section and the `## Completed Milestones` table. Record a decision that widens the milestone's scope by this one sentence, and include the edit in the host-tree rebuild the goal already requires. It is a one-sentence fix in a file whose `/goto-next-milestone` mention sits right next to the skill being reworked. The hosts are being rebuilt and committed anyway, so it costs almost nothing. It also stops the bootstrap from passing a false claim about who writes the table to every new project's runner, just as that skill's done-milestone detection is being redefined. It goes beyond the files the goal lists, which opens the door to other small scope additions. The note's second clause ("Keep both so neither skill fails") also depends on which README structure `/goto-next-milestone` ends up reading to decide a milestone is done. The corrected wording depends on how the done-milestone matching question settles, so this edit can only be written after that question is answered.

Record the stale attribution under `## Out of Scope` and leave `core/skills/init-milestone-base-workflow/SKILL.md` untouched. The goal's file list stays exactly as written, and the fix is left to a later milestone or a submitted task. The milestone stays exactly as its goal defines it: the skill, `docs/skill-reference.md`, `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` and the rebuilt hosts. The bootstrap skill, which changed three times in the milestone that just finished, is not touched again for a problem that has nothing to do with removing the prompts. The wrong note stays in every host tree this milestone ships, including the release whose headline change is how `/goto-next-milestone` treats the README's done-milestone records. A deferred one-line fix also tends to get forgotten unless a later milestone or task actually picks it up.

open-question.question: The goal names docs/skill-reference.md, docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, and the host trees as the documents to update, while CLAUDE.md's pipeline listing describes the skill and its invariants section records every retired interactive behaviour elsewhere as a must-not-restore rule, and docs/workflow.md says the skill advances the pointer. Do CLAUDE.md (pipeline line and a new invariant on the lowest-numbered pick and the retired prompts) and docs/workflow.md get updated in this milestone too?
open-question.recommendation: A pipeline line saying the skill activates the lowest-numbered undone milestone without asking already rules the prompts out, so no do-not-restore invariant is needed, and the workflow.md sentence gets the same wording because it describes the skill's behaviour.
open-question.alternative: Change only the wording that describes the skill: reword CLAUDE.md's pipeline line (and optionally the docs/workflow.md sentence) to say it activates the lowest-numbered undone milestone. Add no new invariant. It is the smallest change that keeps every description of the skill accurate. It also keeps the invariants section, which is already long, for design decisions with lasting rationale rather than the removal of two prompts. Nothing records why the prompts are gone. A later editor who sees an unconfirmed pointer overwrite could add a confirmation back, when CLAUDE.md has written "must not be restored" for every comparable retirement, including the non-committing bootstrap exemption that milestone 35 retired.

Add both files to this milestone's change set. In CLAUDE.md, the `goto-next-milestone` pipeline line would name the lowest-numbered undone pick, and a new invariant would record that pick and state that the retired confirmation and choice prompts must not be restored. In docs/workflow.md, the "advances the pointer" sentence of "Initializing a milestone" would say that the skill activates the lowest-numbered undone milestone without asking. Every document that describes the skill changes in the same milestone as the behaviour, and the removal gets written down as a must-not-restore rule. That follows the convention CLAUDE.md already uses for every other retired behaviour, and milestone 35 did the same thing when its "Update Invariant And Docs For Committing Bootstrap" task edited CLAUDE.md. The work goes beyond the documents the Goal lists, so derive-tasks will only see the extra edits if a recorded decision widens the scope. It also adds a sentence to docs/workflow.md that is not strictly needed, because "advances the pointer" is still true under the new behaviour.

Update CLAUDE.md's pipeline line and add the new invariant on the lowest-numbered pick and the retired prompts. Leave docs/workflow.md unchanged, because its phase-level sentence "`/goto-next-milestone` advances the pointer" and its mermaid node do not describe the prompts and are still correct. The edit goes where the rationale has to live. CLAUDE.md's invariants section exists so that a later editor does not add back something that looks missing, and a confirmation prompt before overwriting the pointer is exactly that kind of plausible "fix". Meanwhile no edit is spent on a narrative sentence that is not wrong. It still adds a file outside the Goal's list, and it needs a recorded decision to do so. docs/workflow.md's description stays generic, so a reader of the phase narrative would not learn about the deterministic pick without following the link to docs/skill-reference.md.

alternative.id: Keep to the Goal's document list

open-question.alternative: Update only docs/skill-reference.md, docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md and the rebuilt host trees, as the Goal says, and leave CLAUDE.md and docs/workflow.md to a later pass. That later pass could be finish-current-milestone's step 7 or a follow-up milestone. It keeps to the Goal as written, so no scope has to be widened or recorded. Neither file is inaccurate today: the pipeline line ("activates an already-defined milestone; requires the pointer to read none") and "advances the pointer" both stay true. finish-current-milestone's step 7 only updates CLAUDE.md for lasting environment-context changes, not for design invariants, so the must-not-restore rule would probably never be written. The milestone would ship a behaviour change whose rationale sits nowhere that editors read, unlike the precedent set by milestones 34 and 35.

open-question.question: The goal excludes directories "listed in ## Milestone History", but that section's headings carry only the integer number and a title (### Milestone N — Title), never the directory name, while the ## Completed Milestones table pairs the number with the backticked directory path. Which structure, and which field of it, does the skill match a milestone_<NN>_<slug> directory against to decide it is done: the number in the History headings, the path in the Completed Milestones table, or both?
open-question.recommendation: It is the goal's own wording, every README the finish skill has ever written carries these headings, and define's uniqueness rule makes the number a stable key, whereas the table is never backfilled, so a missing row would re-activate a finished milestone with no prompt left to catch it.
open-question.alternative: The skill parses the integer N out of each `### Milestone N — Title` heading under `## Milestone History` and counts a `milestone_<NN>_<slug>` directory as done when its zero-stripped number matches one of those numbers. It ignores the `## Completed Milestones` table entirely. This is the literal reading of the goal's "listed in ## Milestone History", so neither the goal nor the skill's current step 2 has to be reworded. It stays correct when a directory's slug has been renamed, because `/define-milestone-goal` refuses a number already taken under any slug, which makes numbers unique and monotone. Every README the finish skill has ever written carries these headings. The number has to be pulled out of two free-form places, the heading text and the directory name, so the match depends on an integer rule that currently lives only inside the branch being removed. How well this option works depends on how the number-ordering question settles. A hand-edited heading that drifts from the `### Milestone N — Title` shape quietly turns a finished milestone back into a candidate. Without the confirmation prompt, the skill would then activate that milestone with nobody checking.

The skill counts a directory as done when its backticked `milestones/milestone_<NN>_<slug>/` path appears in the Path column of the `## Completed Milestones` table. It compares the whole path string and parses no number. The table is the only structure in the README that pairs a finished milestone with its directory, and the finish skill writes that path in exactly the format of the pointer and the directory name. So the match is one exact string comparison, with no heading parsing and no integer rule involved. It departs from the goal's wording, which names `## Milestone History`, so the goal text or a recorded decision has to reinterpret it. It also relies on the table being complete. The finish skill creates the table only when it is missing and never backfills rows, and the bootstrap template still wrongly credits the table to `/goto-next-milestone`. So any project whose earlier finished milestones have no table row would get the lowest of them re-activated without a prompt. A directory renamed after its finish also stops matching.

The skill counts a directory as done if it appears in either structure: its number matches a `## Milestone History` heading, or its path appears in the `## Completed Milestones` table. A candidate is a directory that neither structure lists. It is the safest choice now that no prompt catches a mistake. A finished milestone is re-activated only if both records miss it, so partial tables, older READMEs without the table, renamed slugs and hand-edited headings are all absorbed. It also still honours the goal's History wording. The skill has to state and follow two matching rules instead of one, and it still needs the History number-parsing rule, so it carries the costs of both other options. It also hides drift between the two records rather than exposing it: a README where History and the table disagree is never reported, only tolerated.
